local_access.summary: DSM is fully locally controllable (the DSM web UI and Web/DSM APIs, no vendor cloud required) — deliberately scoped to identify-only here, handing the user to DSM rather than managing the NAS.

device.name: Synology DiskStation / RackStation NAS (DSM)
device.notes:
Synology DiskStation and RackStation NAS units run DSM and are found on the local segment by the Synology Assistant desktop app and the web-based find.synology.com finder, which talk to the on-device findhostd service over UDP 9999 (also 9997/9998). This project does NOT drive DSM (the DSM web UI and its APIs are fully capable and out of scope as home infrastructure). Instead we DISCOVER the NAS, draw a NAS pictogram, and deep-link the user to DSM.
findhostd discovery: UDP port 9999. Synology Assistant sends a broadcast query and findhostd answers with a broadcast reply and a unicast reply. The packet framing begins with an 8-byte magic whose last four bytes are ASCII "SYNO" (0x53 0x59 0x4E 0x4F): the plaintext framing is 12 34 56 78 53 59 4E 4F and the encrypted framing is 12 34 55 66 53 59 4E 4F. After the magic the payload is TLV records (pkt_id / length / value) carrying the unit's MAC address, serial number, model and hostname. This "SYNO" magic is Synology-specific, so a reply that carries it is an unambiguous Synology identification and false positives are effectively nil.
findhostd does not beacon unsolicited — it answers a solicitation — so a consumer either listens for the broadcast findhostd replies triggered when someone runs the finder, or sends a valid Synology Assistant query. This spec deliberately ships NO probe_hex: the full, valid query TLV is not in our captures, and we do not publish unverified probe bytes.
Admin: DSM at https://<ip>:5001/ (HTTPS default) or http://<ip>:5000/ (HTTP default). Both ports are DSM defaults and are commonly reconfigured by the owner.

credentials.notes: Identify-only: no credential crosses to this app. The DSM admin login is entered by the user at the DSM page, which we only deep-link to.

factory_reset.effect: Not this project's concern: a DSM reset (the recessed RESET button, in a mode-1 or mode-2 procedure) is done at the device and clears the NAS's own settings, not anything this app stores. We only identify the NAS.

methods.description: No provisioning by this app. The NAS is set up through DSM's own first-run flow; afterwards it is discovered by its findhostd reply on UDP 9999.

setup.notes: Nothing for this app to provision: the NAS is already on the LAN and answers findhostd on UDP 9999. We identify it from the "SYNO"-magic reply, draw the NAS pictogram and offer the DSM link. Confidence medium: the signature and ports are well documented publicly, but this project has not driven a unit and the exact solicitation query is not captured.

rejoin.notes: The NAS stays discoverable by findhostd wherever it sits on the LAN; identity keys on MAC/serial, not IP, so a DHCP move does not lose it.

testing.notes: No hardware exercised by this project. The discovery signature — the Synology Assistant / findhostd protocol on UDP 9999 whose packets carry the ASCII magic "SYNO" — is taken from public reverse-engineering write-ups and Synology's own port documentation, NOT from a capture we made. The exact solicitation query TLV is not publicly captured, so this spec documents identification by the "SYNO" magic and the fields the reply carries (MAC, serial, model, hostname) rather than a probe we can vouch for; see the notes.
